newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: With peace at stake, N.Korea reports circus fun.
newsitem.headline: With peace at stake, N.Korea reports circus fun.

text.p: On a day that could make or break peace efforts on the Korean peninsula, North Korean state media on Wednesday reported a flower show, a circus and "rhythmic gymnastics".

Fun and games -- and even feasting -- dominated the coverage from the famine-stricken nation as it kept the world guessing on whether it would say yes or no to an offer by the United States and South Korea for peace talks.
The festivities marked the 85th anniversary on Tuesday of the birth of "Great Leader" Kim Il-sung, who died in 1994.
U.S. and South Korean representatives were meeting North Koreans in New York on Wednesday to hear Pyongyang's response to an offer for peace talks.
But state-controlled media of the world's last Stalinist outpost ignored the landmark gathering.
One despatch said North Korean schoolchildren had started annual spring camping holidays.
Another announced the opening of a 100-km (62-mile) long railway line with 10 stations, tunnels and bridges, dedicated to Kim Il-sung.

The only hint of food shortages, which are threatening several million children and babies, was an item by the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) noting with gratitude a gift from China of 70,000 tonnes of food.
North Korea is likely to insist on massive quantities of food assistance as a condition for joining peace talks, Seoul officials believe.
On display at the flower show "were 300 flowers of Kimilsungia and Kimjongilia" -- hybrids named in honour of Kim Il-sung and his son and designated heir Kim Jong-il -- KCNA reported.
The agency described a stage show at which foreign dignatories and diplomats were entertained by "songs, rhythmic gymnastics, (folk) dance, circus and other colourful pieces".
A banquet was laid on for participants in an international arts festival attending by senior members of the country's ruling Workers' Party.

Meanwhile, North Korean radio reported that Kim Jong-il, who has been bolstering his claim to supreme power by promoting loyal generals, was feted by troops on the Demilitarized Zone along the border with South Korea.
Kim Jong-il is supreme commander of the Korean People's Army, but has yet to inherit the titles of state president and Workers' Party general secretary left vacant by the death of his father.
As Kim arrived to inspect a border army unit "a stormy, excited round of hurrahs shook heaven and earth and resounded like thunder", the radio said.
"Such slogans as 'Bullets and Shells' and 'Resolute Defence' shook the mountains along the front."
U.S. officials were cautiously optimistic Pyongyang would ultimately respond positively to the proposal for talks to bury one of the last Cold War conflicts.
But while they hoped for a direct answer on Wednesday, U.S. negotiators were prepared for marathon discussions that may not produce a conclusive reply until perhaps on Friday.
